Thursday, 22 July. The surgery of Dr Lefèvre, a gynaecologist in Croix-Rousse. Ioana has come alone. She hasn’t told Julien anything yet.
Hello, Madame Moreau. Sit down. What brings you here?
Hello, doctor. I’ve been very tired for three weeks. And I can’t stand the smell of coffee any more.
I see. Have you done a pregnancy test?
Yes, a week ago. It was positive. But I didn’t believe it, so I did a second one two days ago.
Positive too. But I wanted to be sure before telling my husband.
That’s normal. How long have you been married?
We got married eleven weeks ago. On 3 May.
Congratulations, then. Lie down, we’re going to do a scan. It only takes a few minutes.
(after a moment) There. Do you see this little spot? That’s your baby. And can you hear that sound? That’s its heart.
(with tears in her eyes) It’s beating so fast…
That’s perfectly normal. You’re seven weeks pregnant. The baby is due in seven months, around 10 March.
10 March… And can I travel? We’re leaving for Romania in three weeks, for a second wedding ceremony.
Yes, no problem. But don’t carry anything heavy, and rest during the journey. How long is the flight?
We get to Iași in three hours, with a stopover in Munich.
Perfect. Come back and see me in a month. And now, go and tell your husband the news!

2. Il y a + past: a moment in the past
“Il y a” + duration = AGO. It refers to a precise moment in the past, with a verb in the passé composé or imparfait:
Je suis mariée depuis onze semaines.
Je me suis mariée il y a onze semaines.
I’ve been married for eleven weeks.
I got married eleven weeks ago.
Je suis arrivée il y a un an.

That evening, when Julien came home from his lesson, Ioana was waiting for him in the living room. She had switched off the television and lit two candles on the piano. Victor was asleep on the sofa, as usual.
“Candles?” asked Julien with a smile. “What are we celebrating? We’ve been married for eleven weeks, not a year.” Ioana smiled too, but she couldn’t speak. She had a lump in her throat.

“Julien, can you play me something? Something gentle. A lullaby, maybe.” Julien looked at her, a little surprised. He sat down at the piano and began to play an old French lullaby, “Fais dodo, Colas mon p’tit frère”. His mother used to sing it to him when he was little.
While he was playing, Ioana came closer. She put a small black-and-white photo on the music stand, next to Henri’s score. It wasn’t an old photo. It was the scan.
Julien went on playing for three seconds. Then his hands stopped. He looked at the photo. He looked at Ioana. He looked at the photo again, as if he didn’t understand.
“Is it… is it what I think?” Ioana nodded. “Seven weeks. The heart has already been beating for three weeks. The baby is due in seven months, around 10 March.”

Julien stood up so fast that he knocked over the stool. Victor woke with a start and hid under the sofa. Julien took Ioana in his arms and lifted her up, then put her down again straight away, very gently, as if she were made of glass.

“Sorry! Sorry! I mustn’t carry you! Did the doctor say anything? Do you need to rest? Do you want to sit down? Do you want some water?” Ioana was laughing and crying at the same time. “Julien, I’m pregnant, not ill!”
They both sat down on the sofa. Julien held the scan in his hands like a treasure. “How long have you known?” “For a week. I did the test seven days ago. I wanted to be sure before telling you.”
“A week! You kept this secret for a whole week? How did you do it?” Ioana laughed. “It wasn’t easy. Especially when your mother phoned on Tuesday to ask me if we wanted children one day.”

They stayed on the sofa for a long time, talking about everything and nothing. The name, the bedroom, the pram, paternity leave. Julien worked out that the baby would be nearly two months old on their first wedding anniversary. Ioana worked out that Radu would still be in Lyon, on his Erasmus.
“Oh no,” said Julien. “Radu will want to teach it nonsense in Romanian from day one.” “And your sister will want to sing it songs all night,” answered Ioana. “This baby will never sleep.”

Then Julien became serious. “And our families? When do we tell them?” Ioana had already thought about it. “In three weeks we’ll all be together in Iași, for the church ceremony. Your parents, mine, Radu, Manon, my grandmother… I’d like to announce it there, to everyone at the same time.”
“Three weeks? Do you think I can keep a secret for three weeks?” Ioana looked at him with a smile. “No. But I think you’ll try.”

“There’s one problem, though,” said Julien. “Hélène and Madame Bernard. They already know, don’t they?” Ioana nodded. “They guessed a week ago, during the fireworks. Before I did.” Julien laughed. “Of course. Those two know everything before everyone else.”

The next day they went up to Fourvière to tell them officially. Hélène was waiting for them in the garden, under a lime tree. Before Ioana could even open her mouth, the old lady held out her arms. “So, my dear? Did the doctor confirm it?”

Ioana hugged her. “Yes. In seven months.” Hélène closed her eyes for a moment. “When I was twenty, I thought I would never have a child. I never did. But today, at eighty-five, I’m going to have a great-grandchild of my heart. Life is strange, you know. It always gives back what it has taken. Sometimes you just have to wait a very long time.”

On the way home, Julien bought a little notebook at a stationer’s. On the first page he wrote, in his beautiful handwriting: “Music for you. First score: a lullaby. Begun on 22 July. Finished… in seven months.”

In the evening, Madame Bernard came down with a bottle of grape juice. “No champagne for you for seven months, my girl,” she said to Ioana. “Doctor’s orders. Well, the former doctor’s.” Then she took a little parcel out of her bag. Inside was a pair of baby bootees, knitted in white wool.

“I knitted them fifty years ago, for Isabelle,” she explained. “She only wore them for two weeks, because her feet grew too fast. I’ve kept them in a box ever since. I knew that one day they would be used again.”
The next three weeks were the longest of Julien’s life. Keeping a secret wasn’t his talent. When Radu phoned to talk about the trip, Julien nearly told him everything three times in ten minutes.

“You’re acting weird,” said Radu. “You keep laughing, and you’ve asked me twice whether my grandmother can knit. What’s going on?” Julien coughed. “Nothing! It’s… the summer. The heat.” Ioana, next to him, put a cushion over her face so as not to burst out laughing.

On the evening of 13 August, the day before they left, Ioana wrote in her diary for the baby: “Tomorrow we leave for Iași. Your daddy has kept the secret for twenty-two days. It’s a record. In three days, your whole family will know you exist.”
